newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish church urges next govt to tackle poverty.
newsitem.headline: Irish church urges next govt to tackle poverty.

text.p: Ireland's Catholic Church said on Monday that record economic growth had done little to alleviate poverty and urged the government that wins June 6 elections to tackle "a deeply divided society."

The Conference of Religious in Ireland, which groups nuns and priests, said in a document sent to all political parties that more people were living below the poverty line now than 10 years ago when Ireland's economic boom began.
"Decisions taken in the past 20 years have resulted in the emergence of a two-tier society," the Conference said, echoing the complaint of left-wing groups.
"Poverty, long-term unemployment, exclusion and urban deprivation are not being tackled effectively," the organisation said.
Arguing that "deeply divided societies are inherently unstable", it urged action to distribute the fruits of economic success more evenly.
Ireland's boom that has earned it the tag "Celtic Tiger" and Prime Minister John Bruton's government says it has created 1,000 new jobs every week since it took office at the end of 1994.
But the Conference contested the figures and said little headway had been made to solve long-term unemployment or to replace part-time work with full-time jobs.

By its calculations, 34 percent of people were now living below the poverty line compared to 30 percent 10 years ago and the proportion of national revenue spent on social welfare has dropped since 1986, it said.
The report echoed warnings by pressure groups and some leading business figures that Ireland's economic boom had left many behind.

Bruton's centre-left coalition, which includes the Labour party and Democratic Left, is seeking to get re-elected on June 6 against an opposition led by Fianna Fail and its ally, the Progressive Democrats of Mary Harney.
Both have made income tax cuts a central promise in their campaigns with Fianna Fail pledging to bring down the 48 percent top rate by five points over five years.
Bruton and his allies say that would reward only the well-off, countering with a promise to widen tax bands and increase allowances to spread the benefit more evenly.
The Conference called for the creation of a body to supervise the prevention of corruption between politics and business.
Last month an official tribunal began investigating allegations that leading political figures in all major parties received large campaign sums from Irish tycoon Ben Dunne
Michael Lowry resigned as transport minister in Bruton's government, admitting that Dunne paid for the renovation of his private home in a complex business deal which is still being investigated.
